$A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2-3\text{i},$
then what is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$" :question/worked-solution "To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =2-3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}2-3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 2-3\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3\text{i} & 3 \\ -3 & 3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}3\text{i}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}+3\text{i}{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(2-3\text{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables to be the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\text{i}{x}_{2}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{i}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}\text{i} \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{\text{i}}{1}=\text{i}.$"} {:db/id 17592186351253 :question/id #uuid "e54214f9-057a-5459-9533-979d032ad9ec" :question/math-academy-id "q-81187"} {:db/id 17592186394119 $$

{:db/id 17592186176678 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176975 :tutorial/content "Let's find the eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-\textrm{i}$ of the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda =-\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} & -1 \\ 2 & -1+\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(1+\text{i}){x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}+(-1+\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since the matrix $A-(-\textrm{i})I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another.

As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
x_2 = (1+\textrm{i})x_1.
$$

Therefore, by setting $x_1\in\mathbb C$ to be the free variable, we find that the general solution to our system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (1+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}]
$$

Setting $x_1=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]
$$

Notice that our eigenvector has complex-valued entries.

**Note:** To check our result, we can show that $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v.$ Computing $A\mathbf v,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Av & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\text{i} \\ 1-\text{i}\end{aligned}],\end{aligned}
$$

and computing $\lambda \mathbf v$ gives

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]
$$

So $A\mathbf v = \lambda \mathbf v,$ as required." :tutorial/id #uuid "1bde3a85-d8df-5194-8581-77fe2108627c" :tutorial/math-academy-id 4297 :tutorial/title "Introduction"} :step/id #uuid "8f4ddd6c-a17e-54f3-bade-a64685e04b36" :step/math-academy-id 26123 :step/next {:db/id 17592186176644}}] :activity/title "Finding Complex Eigenvectors of Real 2x2 Matrices" :activity/type {:db/id 17592186045463 :db/ident :activity.type/lesson} :db/id 17592186176123} {:db/id 17592186176678 :step/content {:db/id 17592186176975 :tutorial/content "Let's find the eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=-\textrm{i}$ of the matrix $[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]$
